articles.description:
Buffered output typically comes in two flavors: fully buffered
and line buffered. If output goes to a terminal then the implementation
automatically selects line buffering, flushing its buffer when a line is
completed so that it reaches the user immediately. Otherwise it fully
buffers, holding output until the buffer is full or an explicit flush
event at some arbitrary point in the future. Line buffering is a common
bottleneck in non-interactive terminal applications such that it’s worth
redirecting output to a file or pipe in order to avoid it. It doesn’t
have to be this way. We can have our cake and eat it, too: promptly
delivering lines to a terminal at fully-buffered speeds.
For example, Info-ZIP unzip prints file names as it extract them from an
archive. This printout dominates extrac…
articles.title: We can do better than line-buffered output

articles.description:
I’ve been fascinated with local LLMs for a couple of years now.
The better open weight models, including some that inference on regular,
higher-end consumer hardware at tolerable speeds, are now reliable enough
to handle simpler programming tasks. This requires a coding harness, but
so far this year I’ve been disappointed by all the harness offerings. For
inexplicable reasons most are built with web stacks, and consume enormous
amounts of memory. At its core a coding harness is essentially curl glued
to popen(). This should not require gigabytes of RAM. So I built my own:
Prospero. It’s written in my C++ style with a snappy Dear
ImGui docking interface. It uses around two orders of magnitude
fewer resources than other harnesses without sacrificing features.

articles.title: Prospero: a new coding harness for a more civilized age

articles.description:
I spent a week creating a new deflate implementation from scratch in C
named tugz to provide an Info-ZIP-compatible zip program for
w64devkit 2.10.1 (released today). I also replaced busybox-w32’s
deflate-based unzip, gzip, gunzip, and zcat apps as well. My new
deflate performs much better than zlib and on par with libdeflate.
In general the new programs are substantially faster and produce slightly
smaller outputs than the BusyBox equivalents, which is optimized for size
than speed after all, but also compared to the original gzip and Info-ZIP
you get in a typical Linux distribution. The tugz programs are
CRT-free (inspect them with peports!) with first-class Windows
support and better Unicode handling.

Besides the cute logo, tugz is public domain and written entirely in my
personal styl…
articles.title: tugz: a new deflate library with three applications

articles.description:
The Nim Team is happy to announce version 2.4.0, our new stable release.
After a way-too-long period of development, Nim 2.4 has finally become a reality. This is a major update
shipping major new features:
--strings:sso for improved string processing efficiency.
--ic:on for parallel, incremental rebuilds.
--mm:yrc, a new cycle collection algorithm that supports cycles spanning multiple threads.
More convenient sum types.
Cyclic module dependencies: still not encouraged, but fair game once you declare them with {.cyclic.}.
If you’re still on Nim 1.6, take a look at the version 2.0 release article to see all the features you’re missing.
If you’ve been using Nim 2.0, the version 2.2 release article shows the improvements available in Nim 2.2.
If you want to stay on Nim 2.2 for now, we also r…

articles.description: LC-3 assembly is an educational programming language. It is simple enough that complex programs can be written directly in it without needing a compiler, and thus it is often used in teaching assembly. An LC-3 textual assembly program is compiled to a binary object file by an assembler, and then executed by a virtual machine. Writing a virtual machine for LC-3 is a fun little exercise. However, in this post, we implement a disassembler for compiled LC-3 binaries back to textual assembly programs.
articles.title: An LC-3 Disassembler in Haskell

Today in the drum class, I gave up playing the song I was practicing. I had already spent three days learning it, and still couldn’t play it properly. In particular, I couldn’t keep the right tempo. I realized that I shouldn’t try anymore, and decided to give up on it.


Work Hard, Dream Big, Never Give Up1

I am largely an autodidact in many interests of my life. I taught myself programming, reading music, running etc by reading books, watching videos, listening to people. A big part of learning by oneself is knowing when to give up. There are many things in my life that I’ve walked way from. Let me list a few2:
Playing video games

As I child I loved playing video games, but upon growing up I decided to stop. I realized that they were too addictive for me, and for the kind of person I am…
